section_summary: This section centers on proposals for a single exchange rate for the Japanese yen, the Young Mission’s stabilization recommendations, and disagreement between State, Treasury, Army, and SCAP over their timing and implementation. Correspondence explains the existing military conversion rate and restrictions on trade, remittances, and converting yen into dollars. Later records address sterling financing, the planned Dodge Mission, and whether Allied missions in Japan should continue receiving yen and services at Japanese expense.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Young Mission recommendations
subfiles.about: Urges adoption of the Young Mission recommendations despite MacArthur’s objections and possible effects on the Ashida government.
subfiles.summary: Urges adoption of the Young Mission report and instructions to MacArthur despite political concerns.

subfiles.title: Information to IATB members regarding Japan’s exchange rate
subfiles.about: Recommends postponing detailed discussions with allied representatives until the United States and SCAP have a position.
subfiles.summary: Recommends telling Committee 2 that talks continue and no conclusion is available.

subfiles.title: Information to IATB members regarding Japan’s exchange rate
subfiles.about: Proposes ways to brief allied trade representatives after the exchange rate mission’s return.
subfiles.summary: Offers a formal IATB briefing or informal consultations with selected missions while the U.S. position remains undecided.

subfiles.title: Exchange rate meeting in General Noce’s office
subfiles.about: Records interdepartmental decisions about cables to SCAP and a deadline for deciding on a general yen rate.
subfiles.summary: State and Treasury secured a delay in the Army’s military-rate cable; participants planned alternative SCAP cables and a decision before July 1.

subfiles.title: Letter to Soviet IATB representative
subfiles.from: Chairman, Inter-Allied Trade Board for Japan
subfiles.about: Acknowledges personal views on establishing a yen exchange rate and proposes circulating them to other board members.
subfiles.summary: Acknowledges the representative’s views and proposes distributing them to other board members.

subfiles.title: Commendation of the Young Mission
subfiles.about: Praises Young’s technical mission report and its contribution to U.S. exchange rate policy.
subfiles.summary: Praises Young and his mission for a clear, constructive report on the yen exchange rate.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about exchange rates for different transactions
subfiles.about: Requests information on rates for commercial, religious, and educational transactions in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Asks which exchange rates apply to commercial, religious, and educational transactions.

subfiles.title: Reply to Representative Fulton on yen exchange
subfiles.about: Explains the absence of a general commercial rate and use of the 270-yen military conversion rate for authorized remittances.
subfiles.summary: Explains that no general commercial rate exists; authorized nontrade remittances use 270 yen per dollar, while trade proceeds use separate accounts.

subfiles.title: Change in missionary remittance conversion rate
subfiles.about: Notifies Pattison that SCAP changed the rate for remittances to Japan to 270 yen per dollar.
subfiles.summary: Reports SCAP’s change of the remittance rate from 50 to 270 yen per dollar.

subfiles.title: Request for sterling agreement
subfiles.about: Requests the overall sterling agreement and asks about dollar convertibility relevant to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Describes sterling arrangements and asks for the agreement to clarify convertibility and potential dollar resources.

subfiles.title: Reply enclosing sterling agreement telegram
subfiles.about: Sends a telegram containing the agreement on sterling arising from trade between Japan and the sterling area.
subfiles.summary: Encloses the requested telegram on acceptance and convertibility of sterling trade proceeds.

subfiles.title: Meeting on the yen exchange rate
subfiles.about: Reports a forthcoming meeting in Draper’s office to consider a draft cable on the yen rate.
subfiles.summary: Reports a July 29 meeting that might reach a final exchange rate decision.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of War Claims Commission documents
subfiles.about: Thanks English for sending documents about the recently established War Claims Commission.
subfiles.summary: Thanks English for War Claims Commission information.

subfiles.title: Commendation of McDiarmid
subfiles.about: Asks Nitze to convey appreciation for McDiarmid’s work on the technical mission to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Requests that Nitze pass along praise for McDiarmid’s mission work.

subfiles.title: Young’s thanks and commendation of McDiarmid
subfiles.about: Thanks Saltzman and praises McDiarmid’s contribution to the technical mission.
subfiles.summary: Young credits the mission’s team and singles out McDiarmid’s work, knowledge, and judgment.

subfiles.title: Meeting on a single general yen exchange rate
subfiles.about: Summarizes the July 29 meeting on the effect of a single rate, subsidies, export taxes, and the proposed SCAP cable.
subfiles.summary: Draper sought more evidence on prices, exports, and food imports before agreeing to the proposed cable. Participants discussed subsidy and export-tax options; Young Mission members were asked to prepare further schedules.

subfiles.title: Army response on general and military yen rates
subfiles.about: Declines the State-Treasury October target for a general rate and urges immediate consultation on a higher military rate.
subfiles.summary: The Army says broader political and occupation factors require further study before setting a general rate. It seeks to implement the agreed July 1 change to the military conversion rate.

subfiles.title: State-Treasury position on yen exchange rate
subfiles.about: Advocates an October target for a single general rate and postponing a separate military-rate change.
subfiles.summary: Conveys the State-Treasury position following the NAC discussion: establish a general rate by October if administratively possible, begin stabilization measures promptly, and hold the military rate pending agreement.

subfiles.title: Suggested public replies about technical mission
subfiles.about: Provides suggested responses to questions about the financial experts sent to Japan and outlines the exchange rate dispute.
subfiles.summary: Advises describing the mission as an on-site study of Japan’s foreign financial relations without announcing a commercial-rate decision. Background records MacArthur’s request to raise the military rate and the State-Treasury preference for a general rate.

subfiles.title: Proposed State-Treasury-Army cable to SCAP
subfiles.about: Forwards a proposed interdepartmental cable responding to MacArthur’s June 29 message.
subfiles.summary: Requests urgent Army review of the enclosed proposed cable.

subfiles.title: Draft cable to SCAP on Young Mission program
subfiles.from: Departments of Army, State, and Treasury
subfiles.about: Argues for implementing the Young Mission’s general exchange rate and comprehensive stabilization program despite MacArthur’s objections.
subfiles.summary: The draft answers MacArthur’s concerns about political responsibility, inflation, exports, subsidies, and control of Japan’s economy. It treats the NAC’s June 28 decision as U.S. policy, seeks an October target for a general yen rate, and calls for stronger wage, budget, tax, allocation, and credit measures. It allows limited subsidies to ease adjustment to world prices.

subfiles.title: Missionary inquiry about using yen held in Japan
subfiles.about: Thanks the Department for the new rate and asks whether his organization may use yen held by others in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Welcomes the 270-yen rate and asks whether private yen balances may support missionary work.

subfiles.title: Reply on private yen balances
subfiles.about: Explains that yen may be bought through authorized institutions, but private sales for dollars are restricted.
subfiles.summary: States that authorized purchases use 270 yen per dollar. Donations of yen might receive approval, but exchanging privately held yen for dollars would violate foreign exchange controls.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about a veteran’s Japanese currency
subfiles.about: Asks how a veteran can exchange Japanese money retained after returning to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Seeks a way to exchange a veteran’s Japanese currency.

subfiles.title: Reply referring veteran’s currency inquiry
subfiles.about: States that the inquiry about a veteran’s Japanese money has been forwarded to the Army.
subfiles.summary: Refers the inquiry to the Department of the Army.

subfiles.title: SCAP telegram on sterling financing
subfiles.to: Department of the Army and Department of State
subfiles.about: Describes negotiations for expanded sterling credit facilities and limits further commitments pending a clearer budget picture.
subfiles.summary: SCAP discusses increasing short-term sterling lines, security deposits, and alternative Exchequer facilities. It prefers a broader credit line but says financing choices depend on purchase, barter, payment, and export forecasts; talks should remain informal.

subfiles.title: Repeat of SCAP sterling telegram to London
subfiles.about: Directs that SCAP’s November 7 sterling financing telegram be repeated to London.
subfiles.summary: Forwards the SCAP sterling financing telegram to London.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about the value and convertibility of yen
subfiles.about: Asks the current value of the yen and whether it can be exchanged for dollars in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Asks whether yen have a dollar value and can be converted.

subfiles.title: Reply on yen convertibility
subfiles.about: Explains that no general yen exchange rate or broad dollar conversion facility exists.
subfiles.summary: Describes narrow occupation-related exceptions and separate trade accounts; no date for general convertibility is known.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about trading with Japan
subfiles.about: Requests guidance on exchange rates, import restrictions, taxes, and repatriating proceeds from prospective trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Seeks practical information before a planned business trip to Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply on Japanese trade and currency rules
subfiles.about: Explains dollar payment arrangements, Japanese trade licensing, and the absence of a general yen rate.
subfiles.summary: Directs Rosenthal to SCAP’s New York trade office for details. Explains that approved imports are paid in dollars through trust accounts and that Japan controls export proceeds.

subfiles.title: Proposed addition to SCAP exchange-rate cable
subfiles.about: Proposes citing British Commonwealth pressure for a single yen rate in a draft SCAP cable.
subfiles.summary: Suggests warning that Commonwealth countries may withhold most-favored-nation treatment until Japan has one general rate.

subfiles.title: Legal Adviser routing sheet
subfiles.about: A largely blank or illegible routing sheet precedes correspondence on Japanese foreign exchange regulations.
subfiles.summary: Legal Adviser routing sheet with no recoverable substantive text.

subfiles.title: Reply concerning 1941 foreign exchange regulations
subfiles.about: States that the Department lacks the requested Japanese ordinances and regulations and suggests the Library of Congress.
subfiles.summary: Says the Department lacks the regulations and refers Seiff to the Library of Congress.

subfiles.title: Request for Japanese foreign exchange ordinances
subfiles.about: Requests ordinances implementing Japan’s 1941 foreign exchange law for a pending lawsuit involving yen-dollar payments.
subfiles.summary: Seiff urgently seeks implementing rules for transactions from July through December 1941.

subfiles.title: Allotment of free foreign exchange to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports SCAP’s possible plan to let Japanese exporters retain some foreign exchange earnings as an export incentive.
subfiles.summary: Reports the proposal and says the Army has requested SCAP confirmation and an explanation.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about funds for a student in Japan
subfiles.about: Asks how H. S. Fujita can send funds to his daughter attending school in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Requests instructions for making an educational remittance to Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply on educational remittance procedure
subfiles.about: Explains that approved banks can convert dollars into yen for limited educational purposes.
subfiles.summary: Names authorized banks and says the likely conversion rate is 270 yen per dollar.

subfiles.title: Plans for the Dodge Mission to Japan
subfiles.about: Describes tentative membership, travel, and subject groups for Dodge’s economic mission to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Outlines five planned groups covering direct and indirect controls, trade, industry, and statistics. Royall may travel with Dodge, while Draper remains the mission’s driving force.

subfiles.title: Forwarding discussion with Netherlands delegate
subfiles.about: Forwards an account of Jobsis’s views on who should establish the yen exchange rate.
subfiles.summary: Sends the attached Jobsis discussion for Saltzman’s information.

subfiles.title: Jobsis on procedure for establishing a yen rate
subfiles.about: Reports Jobsis’s warning against SCAP or Japan unilaterally setting the yen rate and his suggestion to seek IMF advice.
subfiles.summary: Jobsis argues that devaluation after compelled sales of zaibatsu securities could prompt claims and criticism. He doubts Allied bodies could agree on a rate and suggests consulting the International Monetary Fund to reduce the appearance of unilateral action.

subfiles.title: State Department position on Allied mission support
subfiles.about: Responds to Army proposals to end Japanese support for Allied missions and recommends a gradual SCAP-led reduction.
subfiles.summary: State agrees that extensive logistical support should be reduced but notes the missions’ occupation functions. It proposes ending funded yen after an exchange rate is established and reducing procurement demands for missions and occupation forces, while allowing SCAP to manage the issue directly.

subfiles.title: Recommendation on self-supporting Allied missions
subfiles.about: Analyzes SCAP’s request to make Allied missions self-supporting and recommends a reply to Voorhees.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes funded yen and nonreimbursed services supplied to Allied missions. It notes that missions receive far less support than occupation forces, so meaningful cost reduction would also require cuts to the latter.

subfiles.title: SCAP request to end support for Allied missions
subfiles.to: Department of the Army for JCOS
subfiles.about: Recommends making Allied missions self-supporting and requiring Commonwealth personnel to reimburse certain Japanese service costs.
subfiles.summary: SCAP details the authorized yen advances, rising requests from Allied missions, and costs of free services and facilities. It argues these benefits burden Japan during economic stabilization and asks for government-level action to require missions to purchase yen and reimburse personal service costs.

subfiles.title: Army request for self-supporting Allied missions
subfiles.about: Supports SCAP’s proposal to end financial and logistical support for Allied missions in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Royall cites disputes over yen funding limits, the cost of free services, and Japan’s stabilization needs. He asks State to support making Allied missions purchase yen with acceptable foreign exchange.

subfiles.title: Forwarding SCAP foreign exchange controls directive
subfiles.from: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards SCAPIN 1968 requiring reorganized Japanese foreign exchange controls and an independent control board.
subfiles.summary: Forwards copies of SCAPIN 1968 and summarizes its new foreign exchange control structure.

subfiles.title: SCAPIN 1968: Foreign Exchange Controls
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Directs Japan to coordinate foreign exchange and trade controls under SCAP supervision.
subfiles.summary: Orders prompt reorganization of controls over foreign exchange and trade, with clear agency responsibilities.
